analysis.one_liner: Strip legal immunity from websites that knowingly facilitate sex trafficking ads.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 70 Senate cosponsors across both parties and, with only two senators voting no, became law in April 2018 through the combined FOSTA-SESTA package.
analysis.plain_summary: For more than 20 years, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act has shielded websites from lawsuits over content their users post. This bill carves sex trafficking out of that shield: it says federal and state trafficking laws can be enforced against websites and their users, expands federal criminal liability to cover anyone who knowingly assists or facilitates a trafficking venture, and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of their residents. It applies to conduct that happened before the law passed, not just after.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of child sex trafficking or trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, who gain the ability to sue websites that hosted ads or otherwise facilitated their exploitation, and state attorneys general, who gain a new tool to sue on behalf of residents. Anti-trafficking advocates and law enforcement also gain a prosecutorial lever against platforms that profit from trafficking ads.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sex trafficking victims and state prosecutors

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Section 230 of the Communications Act so that it can no longer be read to block federal civil claims or state criminal prosecution for sex trafficking of children or trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion [S3][S4].

It expands the federal crime of benefiting from participation in a sex trafficking venture to cover any person or entity that knowingly assists, supports, or facilitates the violation, so a website that knowingly hosts trafficking ads can face prosecution [S3][S4].
It lets a state attorney general bring a federal civil action on behalf of a state's residents against anyone who knowingly participates in sex trafficking [S3][S4].
The changes apply retroactively, reaching conduct that occurred before the law was enacted [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Internet companies of every size that host user content, which lose a portion of their Section 230 liability shield and face lawsuits, criminal exposure, and the cost of screening out potentially trafficking-related material. Adult services and dating platforms bear the heaviest direct impact, and smaller platforms and startups bear disproportionate compliance costs because they cannot absorb the litigation risk. Consensual adult sex workers also bear a cost: after the law passed, major platforms shut down adult sections, removing tools workers used to screen clients, which advocates and researchers documented as making the work more dangerous.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet platforms, startups, and adult-content hosts

drawbacks.text: The liability carve-out applies retroactively to conduct before enactment, exposing companies to suits over past behavior [S4].

The standard of 'knowingly assisting, supporting, or facilitating' a trafficking venture is broad enough that platforms may over-remove lawful content, including sexual health information and consensual adult material, to avoid lawsuits; this chilling effect on legal online speech was the core objection raised by opponents such as Senator Wyden and digital-rights groups.

After the law passed, major platforms closed adult sections outright; researchers and sex worker organizations documented that workers lost online tools for screening clients and negotiating safely, and several studies reported increased danger for consenting adult sex workers. This is a widely reported consequence of the enacted law, not part of the bill's stated purpose.

Litigation risk falls hardest on small platforms and startups, which cannot absorb the cost of defending trafficking claims the way large companies can, arguably consolidating more online activity into a handful of large incumbents that can afford the compliance apparatus.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real: Backpage-type platforms had used Section 230 as a shield while hosting trafficking ads, and victims deserved a path to sue. But the design is blunt. Instead of targeting bad-actor websites, it reopened liability for the whole ecosystem of user-content platforms, and the resulting over-removal hit not only the intended targets but consensual adult sex workers, who lost the online safety tools studies link to lower violence. The benefit to trafficking victims came bundled with documented harm to another vulnerable group and a lasting narrowing of online liability protection. An honest weighing finds the goals legitimate and the mechanism rough-edged.

outcome.mechanism: S. 1693 itself never got its own Senate floor vote, but its provisions were merged with the House's FOSTA bill; the combined FOSTA-SESTA package passed the Senate 97-2 and the House by wide margins and was signed into law in April 2018.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced August 1, 2017, by Senator Portman and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee [S6].
The committee held a hearing in September 2017 and on November 8, 2017, ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute [S6].
On January 10, 2018, the committee reported the bill with a substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders [S6][S3].
The bill accumulated 70 cosponsors, 43 Republicans and 27 Democrats, an unusually large bipartisan coalition [S5].

The reported version narrowed the original carve-out so it applies only where the underlying conduct violates the federal sex trafficking statute (18 U.S.C. 1591), rather than to any state-law claim, and added a savings clause for pre-existing state claims [S3][S4].

S. 1693 was never voted on by the full Senate as a standalone bill; its substance was instead combined with the House FOSTA bill (H.R. 1865), which passed the Senate 97-2 with only Senators Wyden and Paul opposed and became law in April 2018. The enactment and the 97-2 vote are widely reported but not covered in the provided record.

After enactment, Craigslist closed its personal ads section and federal authorities seized Backpage.com; platforms broadly tightened moderation of adult content. These consequences are widely reported but not in the provided record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's bipartisan sponsors and anti-trafficking advocates got their carve-out enacted, and trafficking victims gained a federal civil remedy against facilitating websites. Internet platforms lost a portion of their liability shield, and consensual adult sex workers, who lost the online platforms they used for screening, are worse off under the law as enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sponsors and trafficking victims; platforms and sex workers worse off

for.name: Rob Portman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in August 2017 and assembled a large bipartisan coalition of cosponsors.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Co-led the bill with Portman and was among the original 63 senators listed on introduction.

for.name: John Thune
for.role: Chairman, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Held the committee hearing, managed the November 2017 markup, and reported the bill with a substitute amendment in January 2018.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Opposed the carve-out, warned it would narrow online liability protections and endanger sex workers, and was one of only two senators to vote no on the final FOSTA-SESTA package.

against.name: Internet Association and major technology companies
against.role: Internet industry trade group and member platforms
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as written, arguing it would erode Section 230 and expose every user-content website to lawsuits, and backed narrowing changes in the committee-reported version.

against.name: Digital rights and sex worker advocacy groups
against.role: ACLU, Electronic Frontier Foundation, and sex worker organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, arguing the facilitation standard was unworkably broad and would push consensual adult sex work offline into more dangerous conditions.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: 70 cosponsors split 43 Republicans and 27 Democrats, and the final Senate vote on the combined package was 97-2, with the only opponents a Democrat (Wyden) and a Republican (Paul).

industries.industry: User-content internet platforms (social media, classified ads, review and dating sites)
industries.note: The bill strips away part of these platforms' Section 230 immunity for trafficking-related claims, exposing them to lawsuits and criminal liability when they knowingly facilitate trafficking. The industry's core interest here was preserving blanket immunity, which runs against victims' ability to seek redress, though the resulting over-removal of content also chilled lawful speech that ordinary users care about.

industries.industry: Adult services and adult-content hosting platforms
industries.note: Sites hosting adult advertising bear the heaviest direct exposure; after the law's enactment, several major platforms exited adult categories entirely. Removing venues that facilitated trafficking served victims, but the shutdowns also eliminated platforms that consensual adult workers used to screen clients.

Not an industry in the conventional sense, but a concentrated group with a direct stake. Widely reported research after enactment found that losing online platforms increased risk and precarity for consenting adult workers even though the law targeted trafficking.
Newer and smaller platforms face the same litigation exposure as large ones without the legal staff to manage it, which tends to concentrate online speech into the biggest incumbent companies.
